body:
The changing pattern of foreign trade

The growth of British manufacturing altered the products India exported and imported. India increasingly supplied primary products, such as raw cotton, jute, indigo and raw silk, while purchasing manufactured goods, including cotton cloth and machinery, from Britain.

This pattern served British industrial interests in 2 connected ways. British factories obtained raw materials from India, and India provided a market for their finished products. India continued to trade with other countries, but Britain exercised considerable control over its colonial trade.

Trade directionTypical productsEconomic significance
From India to overseas marketsRaw cotton, jute, indigo, raw silkSupplied materials required by factories and traders
From Britain to IndiaMachine-made cotton cloth, light machineryProvided a market for British industrial goods

The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 shortened the maritime route between Europe and India. It facilitated trade and reinforced Britain's access to Indian markets.

Surat's decline and the growth of colonial ports

In the earlier trading system, Surat linked Gujarat's textile producers and merchants with West Asian markets. Indian merchants and bankers provided finance, organised supplies and arranged shipping.

As European companies gained commercial privileges and political control, the old trading networks weakened. Ports such as Surat and Hooghly declined in relative importance, while Bombay and Calcutta became major centres of colonial trade. This change reflected a shift in control over trade and shipping, not a complete disappearance of commerce in the older centres.

Modern cotton mills began to develop

British rule did not prevent every industrial enterprise from emerging. Modern factories began to develop in parts of India during the second half of the 19th century. Their growth, however, remained limited compared with the decline of traditional occupations.

The first cotton spinning mill in Bombay was established in 1854. The first cotton mill in Ahmedabad was established in 1861. Jute mills also began developing in Bengal, where the first mill was established in 1855.

Gujarat's connection with cotton production, commerce and trading capital helped Ahmedabad emerge as a textile centre. Cotton mills created industrial employment, although the number of available jobs was insufficient to replace the livelihoods lost across traditional crafts.

Why industrial growth accelerated during the First World War

During the First World War, 1914–1918, British factories were increasingly occupied with war production. Imports of British manufactured goods into India declined, while Indian factories received new orders for cloth and other supplies. This created opportunities for Indian industrial production.

These developments show why deindustrialisation and the growth of some modern industries could occur within the same colonial period. Many artisans had already lost employment, and the new factories did not form a sufficiently large industrial base to absorb everyone.

The rise of Bombay and Ahmedabad cotton mills did not reverse the entire loss suffered by hand spinning and traditional crafts. The location of a few successful factory industries must not be confused with broad industrial development across India.

Prelims focus

  • Surat was an important pre-colonial port; Bombay and Calcutta grew as major colonial ports.
  • The first cotton spinning mill in Bombay was established in 1854.
  • The first cotton mill in Ahmedabad was established in 1861.
  • The first jute mill in Bengal was established in 1855.
  • The Suez Canal opened in 1869.
  • Indian industrial production received a major opportunity during the First World War, 1914–1918.

[Sources: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Ch. The Age of Industrialisation, sections 3.1, 3.3, 4 and 5, pp. 113–123; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Ch. 6, Weavers, Iron Smelters and Factory Owners, pp. 65–74; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Ch. 1, sections 1.4–1.5, Industrial Sector and Foreign Trade, pp. 7–9.]

title: Colonial Trade, Gujarat's Ports and the Rise of Indian Cotton Mills

body:
Meaning of commercialisation of agriculture

Commercialisation of agriculture means an increasing orientation of agricultural production towards sale in markets rather than production mainly for the cultivator's own consumption.

Commercial farming is not identical to the cultivation of cash crops. A farmer may grow wheat or rice for sale, while crops such as indigo or cotton are commonly grown mainly as inputs for manufacturing or trade. The defining feature of commercialisation is the market-oriented purpose of production.

Why commercial cultivation expanded under British rule

Demand from British industries and overseas markets

British industries required agricultural raw materials, particularly cotton and jute. European textile producers also demanded indigo for blue dye. The East India Company and, later, other colonial commercial interests encouraged the production of crops that could be exported or supplied to industry.

Need for cash to meet payments

Colonial land-revenue demands and other financial obligations placed pressure on many cultivators to obtain money. Selling agricultural produce was one means of securing cash. High rents or revenue demands could encourage market sales even when cultivators needed part of their harvest for household consumption.

Trade networks and transport

Merchants, moneylenders and export agents connected villages to larger markets. Roads, railways and ports made it easier to move agricultural products over longer distances. This improved market access in some places while also connecting local cultivators to changes in distant prices and demand.

Important crops and producing regions

CropImportant colonial-era regionPrincipal commercial use
IndigoBengal; later BiharBlue dye for textiles
CottonWestern India, including the Deccan and GujaratRaw material for cotton textile mills
JuteBengalRaw material for jute goods
TeaAssamPlantation crop for sale and export
OpiumBihar and the Benares regionCommercial export trade
SugarcaneUnited ProvincesSugar production

The table identifies important examples; it does not mean that these crops were cultivated only in the regions named. Nor does the production of a commercial crop automatically imply coercion. The conditions of cultivation depended on landownership, contracts, local markets and the balance of power between growers and buyers.

Gujarat's place in the cotton economy

Western India's cotton-growing regions supported the export trade through Bombay and supplied raw material to developing textile industries. Gujarat was connected to this system through cotton production, commerce and the growth of mills in Ahmedabad.

This connection helps distinguish 2 economic roles: cotton cultivation belongs to agriculture, while spinning and weaving cotton in a mill belong to manufacturing. A question describing raw cotton being transported to a mill concerns the relationship between these sectors rather than a single agricultural activity.

Potential gains and limitations

Commercialisation could give cultivators opportunities to earn cash when demand and prices were favourable. However, farmers also faced risks from unstable prices, indebtedness, poor bargaining power and the possibility of a bad harvest.

The benefits were not distributed equally. A cultivator who owned substantial land and could wait for favourable prices had more choices than a small tenant who needed to repay loans immediately after harvest. Thus, greater commercial production did not automatically mean higher incomes for all rural households.

Prelims focus

  • Commercialisation of agriculture means increased production for the market.
  • Indigo was associated with dye production and cultivation in Bengal and Bihar.
  • Tea was an important plantation crop in Assam.
  • Jute was strongly associated with Bengal.
  • Cotton linked western Indian agriculture with textile manufacturing and export trade.
  • Trap: Commercialisation does not mean that farmers stopped producing food grains; food grains could also be sold commercially.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Ch. 3, Ruling the Countryside, sections Crops for Europe and Britain Turns to India, pp. 30–33; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Ch. 1, sections 1.3 and 1.8, Agricultural Sector and Infrastructure, pp. 5–7 and 11–12; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Ch. The Age of Industrialisation, section 3.3, pp. 116–117.]

pictures.alt: Demand, cash obligations and trade links encourage market production, with possible cash gains and risks from prices, debt, bargaining and food pressure.
pictures.caption: Market demand, revenue obligations and trade networks encouraged commercial cultivation.

title: Commercialisation of Agriculture: Cash Crops, Markets and Colonial Demand

body:
Why indigo became an important commercial crop

Indigo is a plant from which a blue dye can be prepared. Demand for indigo increased as European textile manufacturing expanded. The East India Company encouraged its cultivation in India, particularly in Bengal, to supply overseas markets.

For many cultivators, however, the system of indigo production was marked by unequal contracts, low returns and pressure from planters. The way indigo was produced explains how a commercially valuable crop could be unprofitable for the people who cultivated it.

Two systems of indigo cultivation

There were 2 important systems of indigo cultivation: nij and ryoti.

FeatureNij systemRyoti system
LandLand directly controlled by the planterLand cultivated by the ryot
CultivationPlanter employed labourersRyot cultivated under a contract
ControlPlanter managed cultivation directlyPlanter controlled contractual terms and crop purchase
Major difficultyObtaining sufficient land, labour and equipmentCoercive advances, low prices and recurring debt

Nij cultivation

Under the nij system, planters grew indigo on land they owned or rented and directly controlled. They employed labourers and arranged the necessary equipment. Expansion was difficult because fertile land was already occupied, and planters required considerable labour, ploughs and bullocks.

Ryoti cultivation

Under the ryoti system, a cultivator, or ryot, was made to sign a contract, sometimes under pressure, to grow indigo. The planter advanced money and supplied certain inputs. The ryot prepared the land, cultivated the crop and delivered it to the planter.

In the contractual arrangements described for Bengal, the advance committed the ryot to growing indigo on at least 25% of the area of the holding. This was a feature of the particular indigo cultivation system, not a general requirement applying to all Indian farmers or all commercial crops.

The prices paid to cultivators were often very low. A fresh advance after delivery could begin another cycle of indebtedness. Indigo also competed with food crops for fertile land, while repeated cultivation could affect the condition of the soil.

How plantation agriculture differed

A plantation is a large agricultural enterprise generally operated under the control of a planter or company, often employing a substantial workforce to produce crops mainly for sale.

Tea plantations expanded in Assam, while tea and coffee plantations also developed in other suitable regions. Plantation production was associated with control over large areas of land and the organisation of labour under planter management.

The distinction is important: nij indigo cultivation involved direct planter-controlled cultivation; ryoti indigo cultivation relied on the cultivator's land and labour under a contract. These systems should not be treated as identical simply because both served commercial interests.

The Indigo Revolt and official response

In 1859, cultivators in Bengal began refusing to grow indigo in what became known as the Indigo Revolt or Blue Rebellion. The movement challenged coercive cultivation and the power of planters.

The government appointed an Indigo Commission in 1860. The Commission criticised the coercive conduct of planters and recognised that indigo cultivation was unprofitable for ryots. It advised cultivators to fulfil existing contracts but stated that they could refuse to cultivate indigo in future.

Indigo cultivation subsequently declined in Bengal, and planters shifted important operations to Bihar. Much later, the grievances of indigo cultivators were central to Mahatma Gandhi's Champaran movement of 1917.

Prelims focus

  • Nij: Indigo cultivated on land directly controlled by the planter.
  • Ryoti: Indigo cultivated by a ryot under a contract with a planter.
  • In the described ryoti arrangement, at least 25% of the holding was committed to indigo.
  • The Indigo Revolt began in Bengal in 1859.
  • The Indigo Commission was appointed in 1860.
  • Champaran, 1917: Gandhi's movement was connected with grievances of indigo cultivators in Bihar.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Ch. 3, Ruling the Countryside, sections Why the Demand for Indian Indigo, How Was Indigo Cultivated?, Indigo on the Land of Ryots and The Blue Rebellion and After, pp. 31–37; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Ch. The Age of Industrialisation, section 5, pp. 121–122.]
